title: Chanthaburi–Chonburi 3-Day Road Trip: Thailand's East Coast | ThailandAddict
metaDesc: A 3-day, 2-night road trip down Thailand's eastern seaboard from Bangkok. Start at Bang Saen and Si Racha, pass through Rayong, then finish at Chao Lao Beach, Laem Sing, and Chanthaburi old town. Full timeline, seafood stops, and real entry fees.
keywords: Chanthaburi Chonburi road trip, Thailand east coast drive, Chanthaburi trip from Bangkok, Bang Saen Chao Lao Laem Sing
intro: The eastern seaboard is an easier drive than people expect — just a few hours out of Bangkok and you're already at the sea. This route strings together Bang Saen and Si Racha in Chonburi, runs through Rayong, and finishes at Chao Lao Beach, Laem Sing, and Chanthaburi old town across 3 days and 2 nights. You can self-drive the whole trip, pulling over for roadside seafood along the way. No need to rush.

blocks.html: What makes this route fun is the way the mood shifts gradually as you go. The first stretch is busy city beaches like Bang Saen and Si Racha — lively, packed with food. Once you pass Rayong and cross into Chanthaburi, the sea gets quieter, the water clears up, and the crowds thin out. You finish with a riverside old town where you can wander all day. We laid it out as 3 days and 2 nights to keep it relaxed, but if you're short on time you can trim it to 2 days (skip Chonburi and head straight to Chanthaburi).

blocks.text: The route and drive times at a glance

blocks.html: Bangkok to Bang Saen is roughly 1.5 to 2 hours (via Motorway 7). From Bang Saen and Si Racha on to Chanthaburi is another 2.5 to 3 hours, passing Rayong on the way. All up, Bangkok to Chanthaburi is about 250 km. Drive it straight through with no stops and it's around 3.5 hours — but this plan is built around stopping to play along the way, so we spread it across several days.

items: Easiest driving windows — weekday mornings have light traffic. Friday evenings and Sunday evenings get fairly heavy on the motorway, so build in extra time.
Fuel and restrooms — there are plenty of large stations and rest stops along Route 344 (Ban Bueng–Klaeng) and the coastal Route 3.

No private car? — you can take a minivan or coach from Bangkok (Mo Chit or Ekkamai) to Chanthaburi, but reaching the out-of-town beaches without a car is tough. It's best to rent a car once you're in Chanthaburi.

blocks.text: Day 1 — Bang Saen, Si Racha, then down to Rayong

items.activity: Leave Bangkok on Motorway 7 heading for Chonburi
items.note: Getting an early start helps you dodge the mid-morning traffic. There are rest stops along the way for a coffee break.

items.activity: Arrive at Bang Saen Beach, stroll the shore, rent a deck chair and catch the breeze
items.note: Bang Saen is the go-to beach for Bangkok day-trippers — a long stretch of sand lined with seafood restaurants. Deck chairs run about 30–50 THB each.

items.activity: Head up to the Khao Sam Muk viewpoint for a high view over Bang Saen and the monkeys near the shrine
items.note: Khao Sam Muk is a small hill, about 45 m high, separating Ang Sila from Bang Saen. Watch your belongings — the monkeys up there are quick.

items.activity: Stop at Nong Mon Market for khao lam, Chinese sausage, and seafood souvenirs
items.note: Nong Mon Market has been Bang Saen's souvenir hub for ages. The local khao lam (sticky rice in bamboo) and Chinese sausage are what it's known for.

items.activity: Drive on to Si Racha, walk Koh Loy by the sea and cross the bridge for the view
items.note: Si Racha's Koh Loy is linked to the mainland by a bridge — free to walk and catch the breeze, with coffee shops and a market nearby.

items.activity: Leave Si Racha for Rayong, check in near Mae Ramphueng Beach or in Rayong town
items.note: Rayong is a well-placed overnight stop that splits the Bangkok–Chanthaburi run so you're not driving too long in one go.

items.activity: Seafood dinner on the Rayong waterfront
items.note: Around Pak Nam Rayong and Ban Phe there are restaurants with fresh seafood priced by weight. When in doubt, pick the place that's packed.

blocks.title: How to pick a seafood spot
blocks.html: Waterfront places that are busy with locals usually have fresher seafood and fairer prices than spots set up to catch tourists. Check the per-kilo price board before you order — especially for crab and prawns — and confirm the exact weight before it's weighed, so the bill doesn't blow up at the end.

blocks.text: Day 2 — Into Chanthaburi: Chao Lao Beach and Laem Sing

blocks.html: Today is where the mood shifts the most. Once you cross from Rayong into Chanthaburi, the sea gets quieter, the water clears, and the crowds thin out — perfect if you want a beach without the chaos. The Chaloem Burapha Chonlathit coastal road that runs along Chao Lao and Laem Sing is one of the most enjoyable sea-view drives in the whole eastern region.

items.activity: Check out of Rayong and drive the coastal road into Chanthaburi
items.note: Rayong to Chao Lao is about 1.5 hours. Taking the coastal road gives you sea views the whole way.

items.activity: Arrive at Chao Lao Beach, walk the shore, find a seaside cafe
items.note: Chao Lao is a long stretch of sand that never gets crowded, with several seaside cafes along Chaloem Burapha road — easy to sit with a coffee and the breeze for a good while.

items.activity: Visit the Kung Krabaen Bay study center and walk the mangrove boardwalk
items.note: Kung Krabaen Bay is a royal-initiative project with a nature trail on a wooden boardwalk through the mangroves, where you can see fish species and the conservation area. The mangrove boardwalk is free to enter.

items.activity: Lunch on seafood around Kung Krabaen and Laem Sing
items.note: The seafood here is very fresh — crab, prawns, oysters — and usually cheaper than over on the Chonburi side.

items.activity: Visit Oasis Sea World for the dolphin show (if you're with kids)
items.note: Oasis Sea World is in Pak Nam subdistrict, Laem Sing district, open 09:00–18:00. Entry is around 130 THB for adults and 80 THB for children, with scheduled dolphin shows — check the show times before you go.

items.activity: Stop by Khuk Khi Kai and the Red Building, French-era history at Laem Sing
items.note: Khuk Khi Kai (the old prison) and the Red Building are old structures from when the French occupied Chanthaburi. They're close together — a quick stop to take photos and read the history boards.

items.activity: Check in around Chao Lao or Laem Sing, or drive into Chanthaburi town
items.note: If you want to wake up to the sea, stay by the beach. But if you plan to tackle the old town early the next morning, staying in town is more convenient.

blocks.text: Day 3 — Chanthaburi old town before heading back to Bangkok

items.activity: Breakfast in town, then walk the Chanthaboon Waterfront Community
items.note: The Chanthaboon Waterfront Community is a centuries-old trading quarter along the Chanthaburi River that has won a UNESCO heritage conservation award. Walk it to sample old-style sweets and see the old wooden houses — it's peaceful in the morning.

items.activity: Cross the bridge to the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception
items.note: It's the largest Catholic church in Thailand, sitting across the river from the waterfront community. The Gothic architecture is beautiful and you can go inside — dress modestly.

items.activity: Drop by the Chanthaburi gem market (if it's a Friday–Sunday)
items.note: Chanthaburi is a gem-trading city known worldwide. The gem market buzzes on weekends — you can watch the cutting and trading and soak up the atmosphere. No need to buy anything.

items.activity: Lunch on local food — sen chan stir-fried with crab, or sen chan noodle soup
items.note: Sen chan is the chewy thin rice noodle that's a signature of Chanthaburi. Stir-fried with crab is the dish to try before you leave.

items.activity: Stop at Phliu Waterfall before leaving Chanthaburi (if you have time)
items.note: Phliu Waterfall is inside a national park — clear water with lots of soro brook carp. It's right on the way out of town. There's a national park entry fee.

items.activity: Set off back to Bangkok
items.note: On the way back, avoid leaving on a Sunday evening if you can, since the motorway heading into Bangkok gets jammed. Leaving in the afternoon or later at night is smoother.

blocks.text: Seafood and food stops along the route

blocks.html: The best part of this route is that you can eat the whole way, and each stretch has its own specialty. We've listed them in the order you'll hit them, working from Chonburi down to Chanthaburi, so you can pick where to stop as the trip flows.

items.name: Khao lam and Chinese sausage at Nong Mon Market (Chonburi)
items.blurb: Bang Saen's longtime souvenir pairing — fragrant grilled sticky rice in bamboo and Chinese sausage with a nice sweet-salty balance. Eat it on the road or take some home.

items.name: Seaside seafood at Bang Saen (Chonburi)
items.blurb: Restaurants lined up along the beach — order curry-powder crab, grilled prawns, and roe-stuffed squid, and eat with the sea breeze right there.
items.meta: Bang Saen beachfront · priced by weight

items.name: Food at Koh Loy, Si Racha (Chonburi)
items.blurb: Around Koh Loy there's a market and Si Racha seafood restaurants — fresh oysters are the signature of this area.

items.name: Seafood at Pak Nam Rayong and Ban Phe
items.blurb: A midway stop where the seafood is fresh and fairly priced — grilled sea fish, river prawns, blanched cockles. Go for the busy places first.

items.name: Sea crab around Kung Krabaen and Laem Sing (Chanthaburi)
items.blurb: On the Chanthaburi side the sea crab is fresh and usually cheaper than on the Chonburi side. Steamed crab and black-pepper crab are the dishes to try.

items.name: Seaside cafes at Chao Lao Beach (Chanthaburi)
items.blurb: Chaloem Burapha road has several cafes right on the water — sit with a coffee and look out over quiet Chao Lao. A good midday break.

items.name: Sen chan stir-fried with crab (Chanthaburi town)
items.blurb: The chewy thin rice noodle that's a Chanthaburi signature, stir-fried with crab meat and egg, with that smoky wok aroma. Don't miss it before you leave.
items.meta: In town · the city's signature dish

items.name: Old-style sweets at the Chanthaboon Waterfront Community
items.blurb: Walk the riverside old quarter and you'll find traditional Thai sweets — khanom khuang, salted-fish-roe egg cakes, and local snacks to sample shop by shop.

items.name: Stay in Rayong (first night)
items.blurb: Splits the Bangkok–Chanthaburi drive so you're not on the road too long. Plenty of hotels and resorts along Mae Ramphueng Beach and in town across different price levels.

items.name: Stay by the sea at Chao Lao or Laem Sing
items.blurb: Wake up to the sea right there. Great for anyone wanting a slower pace, with beachfront resorts where you can walk straight down to the water.

items.name: Stay in Chanthaburi town
items.blurb: Convenient if you plan to tackle the old town and waterfront community on your last morning — cafes and restaurants are within walking distance.

blocks.title: When's best for the beach
blocks.html: The east coast is good for swimming from around November to May — calm winds, clear water. The monsoon, roughly May to October, brings heavy rain and strong waves, so it's best to skip the water activities then. But even in the rainy season you can still happily hit the cafes, the old town, and the waterfalls.

faq.q: How many days is ideal for the Chanthaburi–Chonburi east-coast route?
faq.a: 3 days and 2 nights is about right. Day one for Chonburi (Bang Saen, Si Racha) then sleep in Rayong; day two for the Chanthaburi coast around Chao Lao and Laem Sing; day three to walk the old town before heading back. If you're short on time, you can trim it to 2 days by skipping Chonburi and going straight to Chanthaburi.

faq.q: Do I need a private car?
faq.a: Self-driving is by far the easiest, since many of the beaches are out of town and public transport doesn't reach them. If you don't have a car, you can take a minivan or coach from Bangkok to Chanthaburi, then rent a car or hire a driver to tour the beaches once you're there.

faq.q: How far is Bangkok to Chanthaburi, and how long is the drive?
faq.a: About 250 km. Driving straight through with no stops takes around 3.5 hours, but this plan is built around stopping at Bang Saen and Si Racha and sleeping a night in Rayong, so it's spread across several legs and you never have to drive too long.

faq.q: How much is entry to Oasis Sea World at Laem Sing?
faq.a: Entry is around 130 THB for adults and 80 THB for children, open 09:00–18:00 daily, with scheduled dolphin shows. It's worth checking the show times before you go so you can time your visit.

faq.q: What can I do if I go in the rainy season?
faq.a: During the monsoon, roughly May to October, the waves are strong and not great for swimming, but you can still happily visit the seaside cafes, walk the Chanthaboon old town, see the cathedral, and head to Phliu Waterfall.
